readerContract.humanQuestion: Anthropic says people used Claude for surveillance, cyberattacks and risky biology. What did it actually observe, and what is still unproven?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: Separate provider-observed misuse from inferred intent and real-world outcome, understand what account bans can and cannot do, and ask a precise question when a frightening AI claim appears.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: No knowledge of threat intelligence, surveillance systems, biosecurity or AI safeguards is assumed.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: A provider report gives a window into activity on that provider’s service: observed requests and workflows can justify intervention, but they are different evidence from an actor’s intent, a completed harmful system and real-world harm.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: A reader encounters a headline saying AI helped build a bioweapon or government surveillance system and needs to judge what the evidence actually supports.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A dated September 10 safety report prepared privately for possible September 11 publication after an actual morning freshness check.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can take the risk seriously without turning a provider’s evidence into a claim it did not prove.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: Anthropic says it disrupted serious misuse on Claude, but the report’s strongest public lesson is the evidence boundary: observed activity is not automatically proof of intent or completed harm.
causalSequence: Anthropic sees account activity on a service it operates.
Its threat team groups patterns into cases and attributes them with stated confidence.
Anthropic can block accounts, strengthen safeguards and share intelligence.
That action changes access to Claude but cannot prove every motive, show all off-platform activity or prevent migration to another model.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A headline says Claude helped with biological weapons; the reader checks whether the evidence was a request, a research workflow, a completed weapon or real-world harm.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: A headline says an AI company stopped state surveillance; the reader checks whether accounts were banned, the system stopped, and another model replaced the service.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: Ask which layer the evidence reaches: observed request, operating workflow, completed harmful system or real-world harm.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; source-linked Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: Use two connected cases to teach one evidence boundary; omit operational biological and cyber details.

analogyPlan.mapping: A venue can remove someone based on conduct it sees and preserve its own records, as Anthropic can block accounts based on activity on Claude.
analogyPlan.limit: A venue decision is not a legal finding and cannot show what the person does elsewhere; likewise an Anthropic ban cannot prove intent or end an off-platform operation.
analogyPlan.whyItHelps: It separates meaningful platform action from broader proof and prevention.
analogyPlan.analogy: A venue can remove someone for dangerous conduct it sees, but the removal does not prove every motive or stop the person going elsewhere.

analogyChecks.mechanismJob: Explain platform visibility and intervention limits.
analogyChecks.reconnect: Anthropic can act on its accounts; the person or operation may continue elsewhere.
analogyChecks.distortionCheck: Does not equate a ban with legal guilt or complete prevention.

discoveryChecks.question: What did Anthropic actually observe?
discoveryChecks.answer: Activity and workflows on its service, not every off-platform act or actor motive.

discoveryChecks.question: Did a biological weapon result?
discoveryChecks.answer: No such outcome is established by the report.

discoveryChecks.question: Did every banned operation stop?
discoveryChecks.answer: No; Axios reports one surveillance platform continued locally with other models.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: The article could repeat OpenAI’s ease and customer claims as proof of accuracy, or imply that permissions alone guarantee a correct dashboard.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: Bind each product claim to current OpenAI pages, bind the missing benchmark to same-day independent reporting, and require the reader action to test one figure and definition.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: A reader can explain why a polished dashboard may still be wrong and can name the three checks before using it.
